title: Agent Memory
body: Agent memory refers to the long-lived state an autonomous agent maintains across sessions, tasks, and tool invocations. The consensus position is that agents should persist memory across sessions rather than treating every conversation as a clean slate. Stateless designs throw away hard-won context on every restart. MemGPT v3's hierarchical memory reports a 40% improvement on long-horizon tasks, and an independent benchmark shows persistent-memory agents outperform stateless agents by 22% on 7-day task suites. Persistent memory is also easier to align via post-hoc audit. Persistence is the default; statelessness is the special case.

title: Context Window
body: The context window is the contiguous span of tokens a model can attend to in a single forward pass. Context rot is the central obstacle to long-running agents, and bigger windows alone are insufficient. A curated wiki is the cure, not raw token count. Context rot is the gradual degradation of attention quality as the window fills with stale, redundant, or contradictory tokens. Karpathy's position is direct: the cure is a curated wiki, not bigger windows. Several researchers claim 10M-token windows eliminate the problem, but the practitioner consensus is that those claims confuse retrieval recall with reasoning fidelity. Agent memory architectures remain essential regardless of window size.

title: Redis Memory
body: Redis Memory refers to the Redis Agent Memory Server, the short-term context layer Redis ships for autonomous agents. The headline result is the 5x lower latency benchmark versus vector-only stores for short-term agent context. The Agent Memory Server treats every agent turn as a stream event and keeps the working set in RedisJSON with HNSW vector indexes alongside. The 5x figure is measured against representative vector-only baselines on short-term recall workloads, and Redis has published the methodology and traces. The 5x benchmark remains the canonical reason teams adopt Redis for the short-term memory tier.

title: Karpathy LLM Wiki
body: The Karpathy LLM Wiki is the proposal that an LLM should maintain a self-updating, Markdown-shaped wiki rather than re-retrieving raw documents on every query. The wiki accumulates knowledge across sessions, is lintable for contradictions, and serves as the durable substrate of agent memory. The shape is intentionally low-tech: one Markdown page per concept, wikilinks between pages, frontmatter for metadata, and a plain-text log of every edit. Each ingestion event triggers a contradiction check; on conflict the page is rewritten and a SUPERSEDES edge is written into the knowledge graph.

title: MemGPT
body: MemGPT is a hierarchical memory architecture for LLM agents. The v3 release introduces a three-tier memory hierarchy — a small in-context working set, a larger recall buffer, and an unbounded archival store — and pages information between tiers as the agent needs it. The team reports a 40% improvement on long-horizon tasks. The core insight is that LLMs can be taught to manage their own memory if you give them the right tools: explicit read/write calls into the recall and archival tiers, and a self-edit loop that decides what is worth keeping. MemGPT v3 ships memory primitives compatible with both vector stores and graph databases.

title: Cognee
body: Cognee 0.5+ is the memory engine that turns a stream of documents into a queryable knowledge graph. The 0.5 release adds a Redis vector adapter, first-class ontology support, and the memify operation for incremental graph enrichment. The pipeline is short: cognee.add ingests raw text, cognee.cognify extracts entities and relations into the graph, and cognee.search retrieves either raw text or graph completions. The important Cognee primitives are the typed edges (SUPERSEDES, CONTRADICTS, RELATES_TO) and the memify operation that re-enriches the graph as new evidence arrives. Cognee also implements a prune operation that backs a right-to-be-forgotten API.
